source.title: Sparse Crosscoders for diffing MoEs and Dense models
source.authors: Marmik Chaudhari; N. Hundia; I. Gulati

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper compares crosscoder features in small dense and MoE models, but does not measure whether neuron poles have one or more interpretable jobs or test the listed claims about neuron explanations.
record.gate_note: The reported feature counts and density comparisons concern crosscoder latents, not neuron poles or semantic interpretability, so they are recorded as findings about a related construct under fits_no_version. The paper does not test explanations on held-out activations or score explanations by predicting activations on new text. Its approximately 87% fractional variance explained is a crosscoder reconstruction result, not a measure of the claim's object, and is not a row.
record.test_reason: The study trains crosscoders on third-layer activations of small five-layer dense and MoE models and compares crosscoder latents: counts and activation density. It never examines individual neurons or neuron poles. It does not assess neuron explanations, simulate activations from explanations, study InceptionV1, or build attribution graphs from neurons. Its results cannot bear on any version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The abstract and introduction go further than the record's paraphrase: they say MoEs develop more specialized, focused representations, while dense models spread information across broader, general-purpose features. They read this as sparsity encouraging localized specialization. The conclusion itself is more cautious: crosscoders apply 'to some extent', and qualitative analysis is still needed to validate semantic meaning.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains crosscoders on third-layer activations from independently trained, small dense and MoE models to compare feature organization. It does not use the neuron-pole audit or test neuron explanations.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that the previously suggested λs/λf ratio of 0.1–0.2 did not transfer well and that a ratio of approximately 0.7 was required in their setting. They also varied the number of fixed shared features, but do not report its specific settings in the text.

fits_no_version.finding: A joint BatchTopK crosscoder with fixed shared features classified 910 latents as MoE-only (Δnorm 0–0.3), 3,226 as dense-only (Δnorm 0.7–1) and 18,940 as shared (Δnorm 0.3–0.7). Some 'shared' latents had decoder cosine similarity near −1.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In crosscoder diffs of small independently trained dense and MoE models, fewer latents are MoE-specific than dense-specific.

fits_no_version.finding: MoE-only latents had higher activation density than shared latents; dense-only latents had lower density than shared latents.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Activation density of model-specific crosscoder latents relative to shared latents differs in direction between MoE and dense models.

record.problems: The models are five layers and trained on around 1 billion tokens, rather than large language models; numerical parameter counts are not stated. The authors say qualitative analysis is still needed to validate semantic meaningfulness and relevance. No uncertainty estimates are reported for the listed feature counts or density comparisons.
record.rows_left_out: No other results were omitted. The reported fractional variance explained concerns crosscoder reconstruction performance and does not measure the listed claims about neuron interpretability.

untested.parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit shares (about 90% one job, 7% two related jobs, 2–4% not understood).
Interpretable-neuron shares across dense and MoE language models up to trillions of parameters. The study's MoE/dense comparison concerns crosscoder latents in five-layer models, not neurons.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neuron, pose as a shared feature, recursive generalization versus superposition.
Effects of architecture, regularization and tools on the share of interpretable neurons, including the vision-model estimates.
Attribution graphs built from a model's own neurons versus trained replacement models.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples predict where neurons fire.
Simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations on new text.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ["none"] and state cannot_determine. They measure crosscoder latents, not neurons, and no semantic interpretability is assessed. The MoE versus dense framing is superficially close to V2, but there is no neuron-level or interpretability-share result. The ~87% fractional variance explained is a reconstruction metric and is rightly not a row. Further method-dependence the authors report: the standard crosscoder overestimated shared structure; the λs/λf ratio had to be about 0.7 rather than 0.1–0.2; and there was no trimodal Δnorm distribution.

versions.untested_parts: Qwen3-32B neuron-pole shares and the proportions with one job, two related jobs, or no understood job.
Whether similar interpretable-neuron shares hold across language models, dense and MoE architectures, or models up to trillions of parameters.
InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose as a shared feature, and recursive generalization versus superposition.
Effects of architecture, regularization, and tools on interpretable-neuron shares, including the InceptionV1-sized vision-model estimates.
Whether attribution graphs built from a large model's own neurons explain behavior without a trained replacement model and its reconstruction error.
Whether explanations fitted to activating examples fail to predict where neurons fire.
Automated scores for neuron explanations based on simulated activations on new text.
